title: Amos 1:1–8
context: The book opens with a heading naming Amos, a herdsman from Tekoa, who received these words about Israel in the days of Uzziah of Judah and Jeroboam son of Joash of Israel, “two years before the earthquake.” The dating and the earthquake are not further described, and readers place them with some caution. Amos then announces that the LORD roars from Zion, and the LORD speaks oracles against Damascus and the Philistine cities, each introduced with a repeated formula of three transgressions and four, for cruelty such as threshing Gilead and selling whole communities to Edom. Place names and historical incidents are held cautiously. Shared ground: God judges all nations for cruelty.

verses.text: The words of Amos, who was among the herdsmen of Tekoa, which he saw concerning Israel in the days of Uzziah king of Judah and in the days of Jeroboam the son of Joash, king of Israel, two years before the earthquake.
verses.arminianNotes:
The heading presents “the words of Amos,” a herdsman of Tekoa, dated to Uzziah of Judah and Jeroboam son of Joash of Israel, “two years before the earthquake.”

Arminian readers see an ordinary man called to speak.
verses.reformedNotes:
Tekoa is usually placed south of Bethlehem; Zechariah 14:5 also recalls an earthquake in Uzziah’s days, though exact dating is uncertain.

Reformed readers see God calling his messenger. Shared ground: Amos speaks by God’s commission (compare 7:14–15).

verses.text: He said: “The LORD will roar from Zion, and utter his voice from Jerusalem; and the pastures of the shepherds will mourn, and the top of Carmel will wither.”
verses.arminianNotes:
Amos says, “The LORD will roar from Zion, and utter his voice from Jerusalem,” and pastures mourn and Carmel withers. The theme is set.

Arminian readers see God’s warning voice going out before judgment.
verses.reformedNotes:
Joel 3:16 opens with the same words, “The LORD will roar from Zion,” though the two books develop the image differently.

Reformed readers see God’s sovereign word shaking creation. Shared ground: God speaks from Zion with authority.

verses.text: The LORD says: “For three transgressions of Damascus, yes, for four, I will not turn away its punishment, because they have threshed Gilead with threshing instruments of iron;
verses.arminianNotes:
The LORD says that for three transgressions of Damascus, yes, for four, he will not turn away its punishment, because they threshed Gilead with iron instruments.

Arminian readers see nations held accountable for cruelty.
verses.reformedNotes:
The same three-and-four pattern repeats through the oracles. Many connect the charge with Aramean wars against Gilead (compare 2 Kings 10:32–33), though the incident is not specified.

Reformed readers agree. Shared ground: God judges brutality among all nations.

verses.text: but I will send a fire into the house of Hazael, and it will devour the palaces of Ben Hadad.
verses.arminianNotes:
The LORD will send fire into the house of Hazael and devour the palaces of Ben Hadad. The ruling dynasty of Damascus is named.

Arminian readers see judgment falling on the rulers responsible for the violence of the previous verse.
verses.reformedNotes:
Hazael and Ben Hadad are royal names known from the books of Kings; which Ben Hadad is meant is not stated.

Reformed readers see God’s rule over kings. Shared ground: no throne is beyond God’s justice, and the fire is a recurring image of judgment in these oracles.

verses.text: I will break the bar of Damascus, and cut off the inhabitant from the valley of Aven, and him who holds the scepter from the house of Eden; and the people of Syria shall go into captivity to Kir,” says the LORD.
verses.arminianNotes:
The LORD will break Damascus’s bar, cut off the inhabitant of the valley of Aven and the scepter-holder of the house of Eden, and send Syria’s people captive to Kir.

Arminian readers see defenses failing.
verses.reformedNotes:
The valley of Aven and the house of Eden are hard to locate with confidence. Compare 9:7 and 2 Kings 16:9, which also mention Kir.

Reformed readers see God directing the movements of peoples. Shared ground: judgment reaches Damascus.

verses.text: The LORD says: “For three transgressions of Gaza, yes, for four, I will not turn away its punishment, because they carried away captive the whole community, to deliver them up to Edom;
verses.arminianNotes:
The LORD says Gaza will be punished for carrying away “the whole community” to hand them over to Edom. Arminian readers see human trafficking condemned.

The charge concerns treating whole populations as goods to be traded.
verses.reformedNotes:
The historical occasion is not stated, and readers offer several possibilities.

Reformed readers see God defending those treated as commodities. Shared ground: both traditions read this as God’s judgment on the enslavement of whole communities.

verses.text: but I will send a fire on the wall of Gaza, and it will devour its palaces.
verses.arminianNotes:
The LORD will send fire on Gaza’s wall and devour its palaces. The refrain of fire repeats.

Arminian readers see the wall that seemed to protect the city unable to stand when God brings judgment on its cruelty.
verses.reformedNotes:
The repeated pattern of fire on walls and palaces gives the oracles a steady, cumulative rhythm.

Reformed readers see God’s judgment as certain. Shared ground: the security of a city’s defenses cannot protect it from the consequences of its injustice.

verses.text: I will cut off the inhabitant from Ashdod, and him who holds the scepter from Ashkelon; and I will turn my hand against Ekron; and the remnant of the Philistines will perish,” says the Lord GOD.
verses.arminianNotes:
The LORD will cut off Ashdod and Ashkelon’s rulers, turn his hand against Ekron, and the remnant of the Philistines will perish. The oracle extends to other Philistine cities.

Arminian readers see a whole region held accountable.
verses.reformedNotes:
Gath, another Philistine city, is not named here; the text does not explain why.

Reformed readers see God’s sovereignty over the Philistines. Shared ground: God’s judgment extends across peoples, not only to Israel.
